chunks: Opto-isolation and its trade-offs. The question: What is opto-isolation? What are its tradeoffs?
An optocoupler is an LED and a light sensor sealed in one package with an insulating gap between them.
Current through the LED makes light, the sensor on the other side sees it and conducts, and no electrical connection crosses the gap.
The main number to know is the current transfer ratio, how much output current you get per unit of LED current. It is cheap and robust, but it is slow, and it weakens with age.
Imagine signaling across a canyon with a flashlight. A friend on the far side has a light sensor and reacts when the beam arrives. The two of you share no wire, only light.
Over the years the flashlight bulb dims, so the beam gets weaker, and the sensor eventually misses it. The sensor is also slow compared with a wire.
Heat makes the bulb dim faster.
Current through the LED (set by R LED ) produces light that drives the phototransistor.
OUT is pulled low when the LED is on and saturated, and pulled to V CC2 by R pull when the LED is off.
The two grounds are separate (the chassis-style ground symbol marks the isolated side). Note the output is inverting with respect to the input.
Optocoupler: an LED plus a photodetector in one insulating package. Phototransistor: a transistor switched by light instead of by an input current.
Current transfer ratio (CTR): output current divided by LED current, I C over I F . Pulse-width distortion: unequal rise and fall delays that stretch or shrink a pulse.
CMTI: how fast a common-mode voltage jump the part tolerates without a false output.
Drive the LED with 5 milliamps from a 3. 3 volts pin and a resistor: (3. 3 minus 1. 2) over 5 milliamps equals 420 ohms. A new part with 50% CTR can then sink 0.
5 times 5 equals 2. 5 milliamps. After years of aging and heat, CTR may fall to 20%, and the same 5 milliamps gives only 1 milliamps.
If the output's pull-up resistor (which holds the line high) needs 2. 5 milliamps to pull the output low, the circuit now fails.
So you design for the worst-case CTR, not the nominal one. That is the whole idea.
"An optocoupler is an LED and a photodetector, usually a phototransistor, in one package with an insulating gap, so only light crosses and the two sides are galvanically isolated.
The key spec is CTR, output current over LED current, which varies with temperature and drops with age.
Trade-offs: slow with distorted pulse widths, milliamps of input current, limited common-mode immunity, and aging, in return for low cost, simplicity and a high isolation rating.
For fast or long-life interfaces a digital isolator is better."
